title: The Map: How the Nervous System Is Organized

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Codex accuracy gate → fixes

cards.front: The {{c1::central nervous system}} (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord.
cards.quote: The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord.
cards.section: A map and its puzzles

cards.front: What single working picture organizes the map of the central nervous system, and what can that picture not tell you?
cards.back: One hollow tube, bent once: a picture of how the CNS develops, not literal adult anatomy. It does not tell you what a region does, or where the blood-brain barrier sits.
cards.quote: Picture the central nervous system as one hollow tube, bent once.
cards.section: A map and its puzzles

cards.front: What three bulges does the front end of the embryonic neural tube first form, and which two of them then divide in two?
cards.back: Forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain. The forebrain and the hindbrain each divide, giving five bulges in a row.
cards.quote: As it grows, the front end swells into three bulges: the forebrain, the midbrain and the hindbrain.
cards.section: One tube, bent once

cards.front: The canal in each cerebral hemisphere becomes a lateral ventricle, joined to the third ventricle by the {{c1::interventricular foramen}}.
cards.quote: so its canal becomes one lateral ventricle in each, and each stays joined to the third ventricle by an opening, the interventricular foramen.
cards.section: One tube, bent once

cards.front: What are the four parts of the adult human brain, and which three structures make up the brainstem?
cards.back: Cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum. The brainstem is the midbrain, pons and medulla together.
cards.quote: So the adult brain has four parts: the cerebrum, the diencephalon, the brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla together) and the cerebellum.
cards.section: One tube, bent once

cards.front: In which gyri do primary motor cortex and primary somatosensory cortex lie?
cards.back: Primary motor cortex: precentral gyrus. Primary somatosensory cortex: postcentral gyrus.
cards.quote: primary motor cortex is in the precentral gyrus; primary somatosensory cortex is in the postcentral gyrus;
cards.section: One tube, bent once

cards.front: In the embryo, the cerebellum grows from the dorsal side of the front of the hindbrain. Predict which ventricle lies directly beneath the adult cerebellum, and what forms that ventricle's floor.
cards.back: The fourth ventricle, the canal of the hindbrain. The cerebellum lies over it, and the pons and medulla form its floor.
cards.quote: It is the canal of the hindbrain, so the cerebellum lies over it, and the pons and medulla form its floor.
cards.section: One tube, bent once

cards.front: Why should no brain region, such as the thalamus or hypothalamus, be assigned a single function?
cards.back: Each region takes part in many functions, and most functions involve several regions. A map names places, not jobs.
cards.quote: Each of these regions takes part in many functions, and most functions involve several regions.
cards.section: A map names places, not jobs

cards.front: One patient has damage to the movement areas of the right cerebral hemisphere; another has damage to the right side of the cerebellum. Which side of the body is mainly affected in each?
cards.back: Left side after the cerebral lesion; right side after the cerebellar lesion.
cards.why: For movement, each cerebral hemisphere mostly serves the opposite side of the body, but each side of the cerebellum mostly serves the same side.
cards.quote: Many pathways cross the midline, so for movement and touch each cerebral hemisphere mostly serves the opposite side of the body.
cards.section: A map names places, not jobs

cards.front: {{c1::Afferent}} fibres carry signals toward the CNS; efferent fibres carry signals away from it, to a muscle or a gland.
cards.quote: Afferent fibres carry signals toward the CNS, as from a touch receptor in the skin.
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: In the spinal cord, why do sensory fibres enter through the dorsal roots and motor axons leave through the ventral roots?
cards.back: Neurons that receive sensory signals develop mainly in the dorsal half of the neural tube's wall (the future dorsal horn), and motor neurons develop in its ventral half.
cards.quote: So sensory fibres enter the cord through dorsal roots, and motor axons leave through ventral roots.
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: Where do the cell bodies of first-order sensory neurons serving the spinal cord sit, and from what embryonic cells do they form?
cards.back: In the dorsal root ganglia, just outside the cord. They form from neural crest cells.
cards.quote: The first-order sensory neurons themselves sit just outside the cord, in the dorsal root ganglia.
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: Where does the dorsal-sensory, ventral-motor plan of the neural tube stop applying, and what forebrain example shows it?
cards.back: In the classical picture it stops at the brainstem. In the forebrain, primary motor cortex lies just in front of somatosensory cortex, not ventral to it.
cards.quote: The forebrain does not follow it: primary motor cortex, for example, lies just in front of somatosensory cortex, not ventral to it.
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: What does the autonomic division of the peripheral nervous system serve, and what are its two parts?
cards.back: Smooth muscle, heart muscle and glands, largely without conscious control. Its parts are sympathetic and parasympathetic.
cards.quote: the autonomic division (sympathetic and parasympathetic) serves smooth muscle, heart muscle and glands, largely without conscious control;
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: Why can the enteric nervous system run local reflexes on its own?
cards.back: It lies in the gut wall and has its own sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons. Many textbooks file it under the autonomic division; the facts are the same.
cards.quote: the enteric division lies in the wall of the gut and has its own sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons, so it can run local reflexes.
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: A student argues that the knee jerk must be autonomic because it happens before the person decides anything. What is wrong with the argument, and which fibres carry the command to the thigh muscle?
cards.back: Somatic does not mean voluntary. The target is skeletal muscle, so the command is carried by somatic efferent fibres leaving through a ventral root; autonomic fibres serve smooth muscle, heart muscle and glands.
cards.quote: The knee jerk is a somatic motor response that happens before you decide anything: the command travels out through a ventral root to skeletal muscle.
cards.section: Outside the tube: the peripheral nervous system

cards.front: In the human forebrain, which way do dorsal and rostral point?
cards.back: Dorsal points toward the top of the head; rostral points toward the face.
cards.quote: So the direction words change meaning across the bend:
cards.section: Naming places on a bent tube

cards.front: Why do 'dorsal' and 'rostral' point in different directions in the human forebrain and spinal cord?
cards.back: The terms follow the neuraxis, the tube's own long axis, not the body. In humans the neuraxis bends by roughly a right angle where the midbrain meets the diencephalon.
cards.quote: And the tube's own long axis, not the body's, sets what dorsal, ventral, rostral and caudal mean.
cards.section: A map and its puzzles

cards.front: You are standing up. Which way does dorsal point in your brainstem, and why?
cards.back: Toward your back. The brainstem lies caudal to the bend in the neuraxis, so it follows the spinal cord's frame, not the forebrain's.
cards.quote: The brainstem lies caudal to the bend, so it follows the cord's frame: dorsal there also points toward your back.
cards.section: Naming places on a bent tube

cards.front: Name the three section planes used to cut the brain and what each separates.
cards.back: Sagittal: left from right. Coronal: front from back. Horizontal: top from bottom.
cards.quote: a coronal plane separates front from back; a horizontal plane separates top from bottom.
cards.section: Naming places on a bent tube

cards.front: In a standing human, a horizontal section through the head runs along the forebrain's long axis. How does the same cut pass through the brainstem?
cards.back: Roughly across it, close to a transverse section, because the brainstem's axis runs up and down like the cord's. Somewhat oblique, since the brainstem is not perfectly vertical.
cards.quote: Roughly across it, close to a transverse section, because the brainstem's axis runs up and down, like the cord's.
cards.section: Naming places on a bent tube

cards.front: In a human, which section of the forebrain cuts it roughly perpendicular to the neuraxis, as a transverse section does in the spinal cord?
cards.back: A coronal section. Because of the bend, a coronal forebrain section and a transverse cord section are both roughly perpendicular to the neuraxis at their level.
cards.quote: a coronal section of the forebrain and a transverse section of the cord are both roughly perpendicular to the neuraxis at their level.
cards.section: Naming places on a bent tube

cards.front: What secretes most cerebrospinal fluid in the adult mammalian brain?
cards.back: The choroid plexus: a frond of capillaries covered by a secretory epithelium, projecting into each ventricle. Most, not all, CSF comes from it, by active secretion.
cards.quote: most of it, though not all, is secreted by the choroid plexus, a frond of capillaries covered by a secretory epithelium
cards.section: The fluid in the tube

cards.front: Trace the net route of cerebrospinal fluid from a lateral ventricle to the venous sinuses.
cards.back: Lateral ventricle, interventricular foramen, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, median and lateral apertures, subarachnoid space, arachnoid granulations, venous sinuses (plus other routes, including lymphatics).
cards.quote: from each lateral ventricle through an interventricular foramen into the third ventricle; through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle;
cards.section: The fluid in the tube

cards.front: In a well-mixed CSF compartment, why does making one full volume of new fluid leave about 37% of an initial marker, not zero?
cards.back: Each bit of outflow carries a mix of old and new fluid, so the marker falls as exp(−t/τ); at t = τ that is exp(−1), about 0.37. Only piston-like flow would clear it.
cards.quote: If the new water pushed the old out like a piston, one glassful would clear it.
cards.section: How quickly is the fluid replaced?

cards.front: Teaching values for adult human CSF: volume about 150 mL, secretion about 500 mL/day, outflow equal to secretion. Find the turnover rate and the volume-to-flow time τ in hours.
cards.quote: Volume-to-flow time: τ = 150 ÷ 500 = 0.3 day, which is 0.3 × 24 = 7.2 h.
cards.section: How quickly is the fluid replaced?

cards.front: In the well-mixed CSF model with τ = 7.2 h, after how long is half of an initial marker gone?
cards.back: Half-life = τ × ln 2 = 7.2 h × 0.693, about 5.0 h. At τ itself about 37% remains, so τ is not the half-life.
cards.quote: Do not confuse τ with the half-life.
cards.section: How quickly is the fluid replaced?

cards.front: A well-mixed fluid compartment of 90 mL is kept at constant volume by secretion and outflow of 0.3 mL/min. A marker is present at time zero and none is added. How long until 10% of it remains?
cards.quote: A marker present at time zero therefore falls as exp(−t/τ).
cards.section: How quickly is the fluid replaced?

cards.front: The cerebral aqueduct is completely blocked while CSF secretion continues. Which ventricles enlarge, and which does not?
cards.back: The lateral and third ventricles enlarge; the fourth ventricle, downstream of the block, does not.
cards.why: Fluid made upstream loses its normal exit, so pressure rises there.
cards.quote: Fluid made in them loses its normal exit, so pressure rises and they enlarge.
cards.section: Block the tube

cards.front: In the simplified obstructive model, a mass completely blocks the right interventricular foramen only, and secretion continues. Which ventricle should tend to enlarge?
cards.back: The right lateral ventricle alone. It is the only ventricle upstream of the block; the left lateral, third and fourth ventricles keep their route to the exit.
cards.why: Rule: a lasting, complete block with secretion continuing tends to enlarge the ventricles upstream of it.
cards.quote: a lasting, complete block, with secretion continuing and no adequate alternative drainage, tends to enlarge the ventricles upstream of it.
cards.section: Block the tube

cards.front: A brain scan shows all four ventricles enlarged. Why does that finding alone not show that the fourth ventricle's apertures are blocked?
cards.back: Failed absorption with open pathways (communicating hydrocephalus) can also enlarge all four. An aperture block does so because all four lie upstream of the exit; the upstream rule does not predict the communicating case.
cards.quote: If absorption fails instead while the pathways stay open, often all four ventricles enlarge together.
cards.section: Block the tube

cards.front: Horseradish peroxidase injected into mouse blood stops at the brain capillary endothelium. What did putting the same tracer into the ventricles show, and why did it strengthen the conclusion?
cards.back: It spread between neurons and glia, reached the outer surface of the capillaries, and stopped at the junctions between endothelial cells. Two experiments run in opposite directions pointed to the same layer.
cards.quote: Two experiments run in opposite directions pointed to the same layer.
cards.section: Where is the seal?

cards.front: Are astrocyte endfeet the seal of the blood-brain barrier? If not, what is their role?
cards.back: No. The seal is the capillary endothelium, joined by tight junctions. Astrocytes and pericytes help the endothelial cells keep their barrier properties.
cards.quote: astrocytes are not the seal, but they help maintain it.
cards.section: Where is the seal?

cards.front: In what sense is the blood-brain barrier selective rather than a wall?
cards.back: Transporters carry glucose and amino acids across, and small lipid-soluble molecules diffuse through. The endothelial cells also move little material in vesicles and pump many drugs back out.
cards.quote: The barrier is selective, not a wall: transporters carry glucose and amino acids across, and small lipid-soluble molecules diffuse through.
cards.section: Where is the seal?

cards.front: Where is the blood-CSF barrier, and why is it not at the choroid plexus capillaries?
cards.back: At the choroid plexus epithelium, sealed by its tight junctions. The choroid plexus capillaries themselves are leaky.
cards.quote: Choroid plexus capillaries are leaky, and the seal is formed by the tight junctions of the epithelium over them.
cards.section: Where is the seal?

cards.front: Horseradish peroxidase is injected into mouse blood, and instead of cortex you examine a circumventricular organ. Predict whether the tracer leaves the capillaries there, and why.
cards.back: It should leave them. Circumventricular organs have leaky capillaries; the cortical result holds for brain capillaries sealed by endothelial tight junctions.
cards.quote: A few small regions around the ventricles, the circumventricular organs, have leaky capillaries.
cards.section: Where is the seal?

cards.front: A tracer in the blood reaches a choroid plexus. Using where the blood-CSF barrier sits, predict how far the tracer gets.
cards.back: It should leave the leaky choroid plexus capillaries but stop at the tight junctions of the epithelium over them, so it should not pass between those cells into the CSF.
cards.why: The blood-CSF seal is the epithelium's tight junctions, not the capillary wall.
cards.quote: The blood-CSF barrier sits on a specialized part of the tube's own lining.
cards.section: Where is the seal?

cards.front: What can a lesion show about where a function lives, and what can it not show on its own?
cards.back: That the damaged tissue contributes to the task, as the rest of the brain performs it. Not which part of the damage mattered, because damage spreads.
cards.quote: The damaged tissue contributes to the task, as the rest of the brain performs it
cards.section: From where to what: four kinds of evidence

cards.front: Why does a neural recording that covaries with a choice not show that the brain uses that activity?
cards.back: Covariation shows only that firing goes with the stimulus or choice. Showing that the activity is used requires changing it, by lesion, silencing or stimulation.
cards.quote: A recording shows that firing goes with a stimulus or a choice, not that the brain uses it.
cards.section: From where to what: four kinds of evidence

cards.front: What does BOLD fMRI measure, and in anaesthetized macaque visual cortex, which neural signal did it follow better?
cards.back: Blood oxygenation. It followed local field potentials, which mostly reflect summed synaptic and dendritic currents, better than spiking.
cards.quote: BOLD fMRI measures blood oxygenation, and in anaesthetized macaque visual cortex it followed local field potentials
cards.section: From where to what: four kinds of evidence

cards.front: What does a stimulation experiment show about a brain region, and what does it not show?
cards.back: That adding activity changes behaviour: a contribution, in that task, from the stimulated population. Not that the region is required, nor which cell type, since current activates a scattered population.
cards.quote: Stimulation adds activity and asks whether behaviour follows.
cards.section: From where to what: four kinds of evidence

cards.front: An fMRI study finds a region active during a memory task, and a colleague calls it the seat of that memory. Which two things does the scan not establish?
cards.back: Which neural signal is active (BOLD tracks blood oxygenation, not spikes directly), and whether the region is necessary. An activation does not mark a region as the seat of anything.
cards.quote: An fMRI activation does not mark a region as the seat of anything.
cards.section: From where to what: four kinds of evidence

cards.front: Recordings show that MT firing covaries with monkeys' choices about the direction of noisy moving dots. Design an experiment to test whether MT activity contributes to the choice, and state the predicted result.
cards.back: Weakly microstimulate MT neurons sharing a mapped preferred direction on randomly interleaved trials, comparing choices at the same motion strengths. Predict a shift toward the preferred direction, not merely worse performance.
cards.why: Interleaving balances slow drifts in attention or motivation across stimulated and unstimulated trials.
cards.quote: Interleaving balances slow drifts in attention or motivation across the two kinds of trial.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Microstimulating MT neurons biases monkeys' motion choices toward the neurons' preferred direction. What does this license, what does it not, and what experiment would test the remaining question?
cards.back: It licenses a causal contribution of MT activity to this choice in this task. Not that MT is the only motion area or that it is required; a lesion or reversible silencing would test necessity.
cards.quote: What it licenses: MT activity contributes causally to this choice in this task.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Where do the corticospinal tract and the spinothalamic pathway each cross the midline?
cards.back: Corticospinal: mainly in the caudal medulla. Spinothalamic: in the spinal cord. (The dorsal column pathway crosses in the medulla.)
cards.quote: The corticospinal tract crosses mainly in the caudal medulla, the dorsal column pathway in the medulla, and the spinothalamic pathway in the spinal cord.
cards.section: Where pathways cross the midline

cards.front: The corticospinal tract crosses mainly in the caudal medulla; the spinothalamic pathway crosses in the spinal cord. A lesion cuts the left half of the spinal cord. Below it, which side of the body mainly loses each pathway?
cards.back: Corticospinal: mainly the left side, since its fibres crossed above, in the medulla. Spinothalamic: mainly the right side, since its fibres in the left cord have already crossed from the right.
cards.why: Trace the body side served by the fibres at the lesion: the left corticospinal fibres have crossed in the medulla and serve the left side of the body; the left spinothalamic fibres have crossed in the cord from the right side of the body.
cards.quote: The corticospinal tract crosses mainly in the caudal medulla, the dorsal column pathway in the medulla, and the spinothalamic pathway in the spinal cord.
cards.section: Where pathways cross the midline
